title: Understand division as sharing and grouping, and as the inverse of multiplication

lesson.title: Sharing and Grouping: Two Ways to See Division

steps.say: You already know that three groups of four cookies is twelve cookies. Today we are going to turn that idea around and ask the backwards question: if we start with twelve, how do we split it up fairly? That backwards question is called division.

Here is the first way to think about division. It is called sharing. Imagine you have twelve blueberries and three friends at the park, and you want everyone to get the same amount. You do not know yet how many each person gets. You hand them out one at a time until they are gone, and each friend ends up with four blueberries. So twelve divided by three is four. Here the three is the number of people, and the four is the answer.

Now here is the second way, called grouping. Same twelve blueberries, but this time nobody tells you how many friends there are. Instead you know each little snack bag holds three blueberries. You keep scooping out three, three, three, until you run out. You get four bags. So twelve divided by three is four again. This time the three is how many go in each bag, and the four is how many bags.

visual.caption: Grouping: bags of 3 blueberries make 4 bags

steps.say: Look at those two pictures side by side. Both are twelve divided by three, and both give four. But the four means something different each time. In the sharing story, four is how many blueberries each friend got. In the grouping story, four is how many snack bags you filled. Lots of kids mix these up. They read a story about four bags of three and then answer four blueberries each. So always finish by asking yourself: four what? Four friends, four bags, or four blueberries? Read the story again and say the units out loud.

And here is the lovely part. Division is just multiplication walking backwards. Whichever story you tell, you can check it with a multiplication you already know. Three groups of four is twelve, so twelve divided by three is four. They are the same fact wearing a different coat. If you know your times facts, you already know your division facts.

visual.caption: One picture, two facts: 3 x 4 = 12 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4

steps.say: So remember: division splits a total into equal groups, and it always has a multiplication twin hiding behind it.

lesson.answer: Division splits a total into equal groups — either sharing it among a known number of groups, or making groups of a known size — and it is always multiplication backwards.

practice.question: Ms. Yuanyuan buys twenty granola bars for the school hike. Story one: she shares them equally among five hiking buddies. Story two: she packs them into bags with five bars in each bag. For each story, work out the answer and say what the answer counts. Try drawing dots in groups to help you.
practice.answer: Both are twenty divided by five, which is four, because five times four is twenty. But they count different things: in story one, each of the five buddies gets four granola bars. In story two, she fills four bags.
